newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Porsche not resting on laurels.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Porsche not resting on laurels.

text.p: At German sportscar maker Porsche AG nobody could blame chairman Wendelin Wiedeking for sitting back, lighting a cigar and congratulating himself for a job well done.
The tough work of cutting costs, formulating a new model strategy and saving the company from collapse in the nearly 1990s is over.

In the latest string of rosy results, Porsche reported Friday that net profit for the first half of this year nearly quadrupled to 38.4 million marks ($23 million) and the company predicted sales for the year ending July 31 of 3.5 billion marks, up from 2.1 billion marks the year before.

"In view of the expanding business developments and a better cost structure, we expect strong improvements in Porsche's earnings in coming years," Vereinsbank car analyst Georg Stuerzer wrote in a commentary on the company.

The figures follow a sharp increase in profits last year to 48.1 million marks and, according to analysts, helped confirm Porsche's place as one of corporate Germany's real success stories of the 1990s.

But far from resting on his lauerls, Wiedeking is pushing Porsche into new markets far from its traditional sportscar history in an attempt to ensure that today's success does not become tomorrow's failure.
"At the moment everything is going well, but Porsche wants to be ready for the long-term," spokesman Michael Shimpke said.

All too aware of the fickleness of the sports car market and its largest customer base in the U.S., Wiedeking has considered a variety of strategies to balance the company's product line which now consists of only two cars -- the two-seat Boxster and its stalwart 911 model.

But in the next test of his guideance of Porsche, Wiedeking appears to be committing the company to press ahead with developing a sports utility vehicle -- the company's first foray outside the sportscar world.
Porsche had hoped to develop the car with fellow Stuttgart carmaker, Mercedes-Benz, but Mercedes pulled out of the project last month due to fears it would not be profitable enough.
Undeterred, Wiedeking says he will develop the car on his own if he has to. "We have learned about the market and the technology involved from our talks with Mercedes," Schimpke said.
Porsche's commitment to broadening its product line follows another controversial move -- a decision last month to build at least some of its fast-selling Boxster models in Finland.
The move was meant to see the company through a production bottle-neck, but marks a break with an industry trend of consolidating production.
Indeed, the deal was even more surprising because Porsche passed over a chance to have Wilhelm Karmann GmbH make the car closer to home.
"It is a clear indication that everyone at Porsche is confident that they can sell every car they make," said Peter Schmidt, analyst at Automotive Inustry Data.
And why not. The profit announced on Friday was more than two million marks higher than the company's own projection in late January and unit car sales surged 32.7 percent to 13,549.
Indeed, the first new model under Wiedeking's five-year tenure, the Boxster, has sold better than any one had expected, pushing Porsche's main plant to full production.
The 911 model, more than 30-years old, meanwhile, continues to sell well thanks to continued upgrades that have left it one of the most advanced sportscars on the road.
